1.title: Context Engineering
1.text: Welcome to Module nine: Context Engineering. This module covers the skills context engineering. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Context engineering: deciding what goes into the context window, in what order, and for how long. Preventing context drift and bloat: tool output pruning and compaction. Context isolation with subagents or multi-step workflows. Memory outside the window.

1.title: Case Check-In: Tidewater's Assistant Gets Confused Late in the Day
1.text: Our running case is Tidewater Insurance. Tidewater's Assistant Gets Confused Late in the Day. Adjusters keep one long session open all day. Each question pulls in large policy lookups and forty-field claim records. By afternoon the assistant repeats itself, ignores early instructions and costs more per question.

1.title: The Context Is a Budget
1.text: The Context Is a Budget. The figure shows this: The context window is a budget: tool results and history grow until they crowd out what matters; prune, compact, isolate and store outside. Everything in the window competes for attention: system prompt, instructions, tool definitions, history, documents and tool results. More is not better; relevant and well ordered is better. Context drift: the model gradually loses track of early instructions or facts as the window fills with later material.

1.title: The Context Is a Budget, continued
1.text: The Context Is a Budget, continued. Context bloat: tokens spent on irrelevant content (verbose tool output, stale history) raise cost and latency and lower quality. Exam tip: Context problems (drift, repetition, rising cost) are fixed by managing the context, not by buying a bigger window.

1.title: Techniques
1.text: Techniques. Tool output pruning. What it does: Trim tool results to the fields that matter before they enter the context; or clear old tool results (context editing). Use when: A tool returns far more than the next step needs. Compaction (summarization). What it does: Replace older turns with a summary (server-side compaction, or your own summarizing call). Use when: A long conversation nears the limit. Context isolation. What it does: Do verbose work in a subagent or a separate step and bring back a short result. Use when: Exploration, search or analysis would flood the main context.

1.title: Techniques, continued
1.text: Techniques, continued. Multi-step workflows. What it does: Break work into steps, each with only the context it needs. Use when: A single huge prompt is slow, costly and hard to debug. External memory. What it does: Save key facts to files or a store and load them when relevant (a memory tool). Use when: Facts must survive beyond the window or across sessions. Retrieval just in time. What it does: Fetch documents when needed instead of loading everything up front. Use when: Large corpora. Ordering. What it does: Put long documents first and the question and instructions last; keep stable content before volatile content (caching). Use when: Long-context prompts.

1.title: Techniques, continued
1.text: Techniques, continued. The figure shows this: Prune tool output, compact old turns, isolate verbose work in subagents, and keep durable facts in external memory. Compaction risks: a summary can lose exact numbers, dates and commitments. Keep such facts in a separate persistent block that is re-sent each turn, and test what the summary preserves. Do not drop what the next step needs; prune by relevance, not just by age.

1.title: Techniques, continued
1.text: Techniques, continued. Session hygiene helps: a fresh session per task is the cheapest context management (Module four). The A P I (application programming interface) offers server-side compaction (beta) for long conversations and context editing to clear old tool results; models differ in whether they track their remaining context. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Symptoms of drift and bloat (ignores early rules, repeats itself, slow and costly) point to pruning, compaction, isolation or a fresh session, not to a bigger model. Exam tip: Exact figures and commitments must not pass through a summary: keep them in a separate persistent block.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Context: A budget: everything competes for attention, cost and latency. Drift or bloat: Early rules ignored, repetition or irrelevant tokens, higher cost. Pruning: Trim or clear tool results; keep only fields the next step needs. Compaction: Summarize older turns; keep exact facts in a separate block. Isolation: Subagents or separate steps return short results. Memory: External files or store; load when relevant. Ordering: Long documents first, question last; stable before volatile. Hygiene: Fresh session per task.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Late in a long session the assistant ignores early instructions and each answer is slower and costlier. What is the most direct improvement? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Drift and bloat come from a crowded context; reduce and reorganize what the model has to carry.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A tool returns forty fields per claim, but only five matter for the next step. What should the developer do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Tool output pruning keeps the window lean without losing what the next step needs.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A long conversation will soon exceed the context window. Which technique replaces older turns with a shorter version? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Compaction summarizes older history into a shorter form, which frees room in the window for new turns.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. After compaction the assistant forgets an exact deductible amount a customer stated earlier. What is the best remedy? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Critical exact facts should not pass through summarization.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. An exploration task reads dozens of files and would flood the main conversation. What is a good design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Isolation keeps verbose work out of the main context.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. For a prompt with a long contract and a question about it, how should the content be ordered? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Putting long material first and the query last generally improves results.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. Select two. Which two belong to good context engineering? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. Retrieve just in time and use external memory; keep stable text first for caching.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all seven answers. Question one: D. Question two: C. Question three: A. Question four: D. Question five: B. Question six: A. Question seven: B and D. In the next module, we continue the course.
